title: The Clockmaker of Stolen Hours
summary: In the town of Greyhollow, the clocks begin running backward and people forget the things they love. Tomás, a clockmaker's apprentice, is the only one who notices — because he's the only one who hasn't forgotten yet.

chapters.title: The Bell That Struck Thirteen
chapters.body:
Greyhollow was a town built around a bell. The great bell in the square's tower had marked the hours since before any grandfather could remember, and all of Greyhollow's life turned around it: the bakeries opened on the first stroke, the schools on the eighth, and the lights went out when it struck ten at night. The people of Greyhollow were proud of their punctuality. They said that in a town of punctual people nothing bad could ever happen, because bad things are always late or in a hurry, and never arrive right on time.

Tomás was apprentice to the old clockmaker Mr. Aurelio, whose workshop sat right beneath the tower. He was a boy of quick fingers and slow patience, which made for a good clockmaker. He spent his days among tiny gears, springs thin as hairs, and the tick-tock of a hundred clocks that never quite agreed with one another but that Mr. Aurelio kept in harmony the way a conductor keeps an orchestra.

On a foggy Tuesday, the great bell struck thirteen times.

Tomás counted. He counted again. Thirteen. He looked at Mr. Aurelio, waiting for the old man to laugh and say what a silly boy, bells don't strike thirteen. But Mr. Aurelio had gone white as wax, the winding key frozen in the air.

"Did you count?" the old man asked, quietly.

"Thirteen," said Tomás.

"And do you remember counting?"

The question was strange, but Tomás answered that yes, he remembered, he had counted on his own fingers. Mr. Aurelio let out his breath like someone receiving news that was both bad and very old at once.

"Then there's still time," he said. "But not much."

That afternoon, Tomás began to notice things gone wrong. The baker, Mrs. Ciça, forgot to open the bakery — she who had opened on the first stroke for forty years. When Tomás knocked to remind her, she looked at him, confused, and asked what bakery, she had never baked bread in her life. But the smell of yeast was soaked into the walls, into her clothes, into the furniture. Her body remembered the bread. Only her mind had forgotten.

The corner clockwinder forgot the way home. The teacher forgot the names of his own students. And, most frightening of all, no one found it strange. They forgot, and forgot too that they had forgotten, and carried on with a hole where a loved thing used to be, feeling no loss, because the loss had gone as well.

Tomás ran back to the workshop.

"People are forgetting," he said, out of breath.

"They're being robbed," corrected Mr. Aurelio. He was sitting in the dark, and for the first time in all those years he looked truly old, and afraid. "Listen carefully, Tomás, because I don't know how much longer I'll remember this to tell you. There is a thing that feeds on hours. On time. It lives in stopped clocks, in the hours people waste, in the minutes we spend without paying attention to our lives. Long ago, the founders of Greyhollow trapped it inside the great bell, and made the bell strike without pause, right on time, so that it would never have a single second of silence in which to escape."

"The bell struck thirteen," said Tomás.

"The bell struck thirteen," the old man repeated, "because it stole an hour. And with each hour it steals, it grows stronger, and steals faster. Tomorrow it will steal two. Then four. And when it has stolen enough time…"

Mr. Aurelio stopped. He frowned. He looked at Tomás with a sudden, terrible doubt in his eyes.

"I'm sorry, boy," he said. "Who are you again?"

chapters.title: The Stair Inside the Bell
chapters.body:
Mr. Aurelio had forgotten Tomás.

The boy stood in the middle of the workshop, surrounded by a hundred clocks that now, he realized, were all running backward. The hands turned in reverse, slowly, stealing time in silence. The old clockmaker went on sitting there, smiling politely at the stranger in his workshop, offering tea, with no idea that the stranger was the boy he had raised like a grandson.

Tomás wanted to cry. But crying took time, and time was exactly what the thing wanted. So instead, he thought. He thought fast, the way Mr. Aurelio had taught him: when a mechanism jams, don't force it. Find the right gear and move only that one.

If the thing grew stronger by stealing hours, and if it was trapped in the bell, then it was the bell he had to enter. And if everyone in Greyhollow was forgetting, but he was not, there was a reason. Tomás thought about what the old man had said: the thing feeds on the minutes we spend without paying attention to our lives. Tomás was a clockmaker's apprentice. He spent his days paying attention to tiny things, counting seconds, listening to the tick-tock. He noticed time. And so time, perhaps, could not be stolen from him so easily.

It was the only advantage he had. It would have to be enough.

The door to the bell tower had been locked for generations, but Tomás was a clockmaker, and locks are only clocks that make no sound. He knelt, took from his pocket the thin hooks he used for stuck springs, and worked the lock with cold fingers until it gave with a dry click. The door opened onto a stone staircase that spiraled up into the dark, and from above came the enormous tick-tock of the bell's great mechanism — only it, too, now ran backward.

Tomás climbed. With each step, the air grew colder and heavier, as if time itself pooled there, thick as old honey. And with each step, he felt the thing trying to get into his head. It came in the form of forgettings: suddenly he couldn't remember his mother's face. Then the name of the street where he lived. Then why he was climbing that staircase.

But each time a forgetting arrived, Tomás did something that Mr. Aurelio, without knowing it, had taught him his whole life. He paid attention. He stopped. He breathed. He said aloud something true: "My name is Tomás. My mother had a leaf-shaped birthmark on her wrist. Mr. Aurelio called me 'boy' and ruffled my hair when I got a repair right." And, saying it aloud, he fastened the memory back in place, like someone tightening a screw that was working loose.

The thing did not like this. The walls groaned. The cold bit.

At the top of the stair was a chamber, and at the center of the chamber was the heart of the great bell: an enormous gear, the size of a mill wheel, with bronze teeth each bigger than Tomás. And coiled around it, like a shadow that had grown a body, was the thing that ate time. It had no fixed shape. It was made of clock hands and forgetting, of all the stolen hours, and where a face should have been there was only a numberless clock dial, with two hands that turned searching for someone to point at.

The hands found Tomás. They stopped. They pointed at him.

"You pay too much attention," said the thing, and its voice was the sound of a thousand clocks striking the wrong hour at once. "That's a nuisance. But don't worry. I have all the time in the world. Literally. And you, boy, have less and less."

The great gear turned backward with a groan of metal, and Tomás felt his own years begin to drain out of him, like sand from a cracked hourglass.

chapters.title: Right on Time
chapters.body:
Tomás felt himself growing smaller. Not in size — in time. The thing was drawing out his years, and with each second he remembered less, knew less, was less. His hands, which knew how to fix a hundred clocks, began to forget how to move. Soon he would forget even how to breathe.

But clockmakers, even apprentices, know something the thing that eats time never understood: time is not only something you spend. It is something you mark. And to mark time — to strike it right on the hour, firmly, without delay — is the exact opposite of wasting it.

The thing had been trapped there for generations because the bell struck right on time, without pause. As long as the bell marked time properly, it had not a single second of silence to escape in or to fatten on. It had only grown strong now because the mechanism, contaminated by it, had begun to run backward — to mark the wrong time.

Tomás did not need to destroy the thing. He couldn't. You don't destroy forgetting; it is too large and too old. But you can do something simpler and more stubborn: you can set the clock right.

With the last of his strength, with the last of the years left to him, Tomás did not run from the great gear. He ran to it. He grabbed the nearest bronze tooth — cold, slippery, heavy as the world — and pushed. He pushed in the right direction. Against the current. Making the mechanism, which was running backward, hesitate.

"What are you doing?" the thing grated, and for the first time there was something in its voice that was not contempt. It was fright.

"Setting the clock right," said Tomás, through clenched teeth.

He pushed again. The gear stopped turning backward. It shuddered, caught between the two directions — the backward of the thing and the forward of a stubborn boy who refused to forget. Tomás thought of his mother, of the leaf-shaped mark. He thought of Mr. Aurelio ruffling his hair. He thought of Mrs. Ciça and the smell of bread her body did not forget. He paid attention to each of these things with all the strength he had, and turned that attention into muscle, and pushed.

The great gear gave — and turned forward.

One tooth caught. Then another. The whole mechanism, with a crash that shook the tower to its base, took up the old, right rhythm again. And the great bell struck.

Once. On the exact hour.

The sound passed through the thing the way a lighthouse beam passes through the dark. It could not exist where time was marked properly. Each right stroke pressed it back, into the mechanism, into the silence between the seconds, where it would be trapped again as long as the bell struck on the hour — which is to say, forever, if the clockmakers of Greyhollow did their work.

The bell struck twelve times, noon, the right hour. And with each stroke, far below in the town, people stopped in the middle of the street, blinked, and remembered. Mrs. Ciça felt a sudden, enormous, unexplainable longing for the smell of yeast, and ran back to the bakery. The teacher remembered the name of every student all at once, and had to sit down. And Mr. Aurelio, in the workshop beneath the tower, raised his head, looked at the door as if expecting someone, and said, without quite knowing why:

"The boy. Where's the boy?"

Tomás came down the stairs slowly, with his years back in place, tired as someone who has lived a day of a thousand hours. He entered the workshop. Mr. Aurelio looked at him — and knew him.

"Tomás," said the old man, and the word was the most beautiful sound in the world. "You've arrived right on time."

"Always," said Tomás. "I'm a clockmaker."
